title: The Practice Ladder
seoTitle: How to Practise Tennis in 5 Steps | Amir Ardekanian
description: Drills, rallies, practice points, practice matches and competitions. Why a competitive tennis player needs all five, in order, and what the research says.

blocks.text: Most players practise tennis one way. Some hit basket after basket with a coach. Others only play sets. A 2007 review of tennis practice said both leave learning short of its best.
I tell the competitive players I coach to practise in five different ways, and to do them in order. Each step works on the same skill. Each one asks more of your head than the one before.
Here's the ladder and why each step is on it. I'll also tell you what the research does and doesn't show. I use tennis examples, but padel works the same way.
The five steps
Pick one thing you're working on, like your kick serve or your backhand slice. Then take that one thing up the ladder.

blocks.label: Step 1 — Coached drills
blocks.text: Your coach feeds you balls from a basket and you work on the technique. You know where the ball is coming. There's no opponent and no score.

blocks.label: Step 2 — Rallies
blocks.text: The same thing with a live ball and a partner. The ball doesn't always come where you want it, so you have to adjust.

blocks.label: Step 3 — Practice points
blocks.text: The same thing again, but now you play points. You choose the shot, and the score matters a little.

blocks.label: Step 4 — Practice matches
blocks.text: The same thing in a full match against someone who wants to win. Nothing is on the line.

blocks.label: Step 5 — Competitions
blocks.text: The same thing when the result counts.
The skill stays the same all the way up. What changes is how much your head has to do.
What changes on each step
Every step up adds something the step below can't give you.

items: What you can see. A basket feed has no body behind it. A real opponent shows you where the ball is going before it leaves the racket.
What you have to decide. A drill tells you what to hit. Points and matches don't.
What's at stake. Miss in a drill and you hit another one. Miss in a match and you lose the point.

blocks.text: Take one of these away and you're training a different skill. A serve to an empty box isn't the same job as a serve to someone who's about to return it.

blocks.label: The research
blocks.text: In a six-week study, 33 junior players practised serving in one of three ways: to nobody, to a returner, or to a returner plus one more shot. More match-like practice didn't simply mean a better serve. The groups behaved differently in matches. On second serves, the group with the most match-like practice went for placement. The other two went for speed. A second study found that elite juniors spent under 13% of their practice time on serve and return, and mostly practised each one on its own.
Why you start with drills
A new shot, or a change to an old one, is hard on its own. Your head can only hold so much. Try to fix your grip and read your opponent at the same time, and something drops.
So you start where the load is lowest. That's the coached drill. You can think about the movement and nothing else.

blocks.label: The research
blocks.text: Blocked practice is all your forehands, then all your backhands. In a study of 83 college students in tennis classes, the weaker players learned groundstrokes better that way than from mixed practice. For the stronger players it made no difference. In a golf and basketball study, beginners did best when they started with repetition and moved step by step to mixed practice. That beat staying with repetition. It also beat mixing from the first day.
Don't overdo the mixing, either. A 2024 review of 54 studies found that mixed practice beats repetition in lab tasks. In real sport and PE settings the gain was small and not reliable.

Thinking about the movement helps while a skill is new. In studies with golfers and soccer players, thinking step by step helped beginners, and helped experts on their weaker side. It made their best, well-learned skills worse.
That's the reason for the order. The first step is where you think about it. The later steps are where you stop.
Why you can't stay on the first step
A basket session feels great. The balls land where you want them and the shot looks good. That's the trap.

blocks.label: The research
blocks.text: Researchers have known for decades that how you perform during practice is often a poor guide to what you've learned. A clean drill shows you can do it now, in these conditions. It doesn't show you can do it next week against an opponent.

Games don't replace drills, though. A 2020 review of mostly school and university studies found that teaching through games improved decision making more than technical teaching did. It didn't clearly improve skill execution. A 2021 review of 34 soccer papers found that game-like practice with room to explore improved technique and tactics, and that plain repetition improved technique too. What repetition does to match play, nobody knows yet.
Why you can't skip to matches
A match asks a lot of your head. You're reading an opponent, picking tactics, keeping score and dealing with nerves, all while you hit the ball. A shot you haven't fully learned suffers most.

blocks.label: The research
blocks.text: In a table tennis study, players returned balls from a machine while doing a memory task in their heads. Experts lost about 10% of their performance. Novices lost 30 to 50%.

Pressure is its own load. A 2021 review of 14 studies found that practising under pressure improved performance under pressure, in beginners and experienced performers alike. The authors' advice was to build pressure into training instead of just doing more training. I go deeper on this in Practise Under Pressure.
What nobody has tested
Here's the honest part. I found no study that tests this exact ladder, step by step. And no study tells you how much time each step should get.
What the studies do give you are the pieces.

items: Take the opponent out and you learn something different.
Easy practice often feels better than it works.
Pressure needs practice of its own.
No one way of practising covers all of it.

blocks.text: How you split your time depends on the player and the skill. Someone rebuilding a serve needs more of the early steps. Someone who plays well and loses the close ones needs more of the last two.
Check your week
Write down your last two weeks of tennis. Next to each session, mark which step it was.

items: Which step has most of your hours?
Does the skill you're working on show up on more than one step, or does every session train something different?
Do you play competitions, or only practice matches?

blocks.text: Fill the empty step first. Then take one skill all the way up.

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Take one skill up the whole ladder. If it falls apart on a step, drop back one and make it solid there before you climb again.

Based on Reid et al. (2007), Krause et al. (2019, two studies), Hebert et al. (1996), Porter and Magill (2010), Czyż et al. (2024), Beilock et al. (2002), Soderstrom and Bjork (2015), Abad Robles et al. (2020), Bergmann et al. (2021), Schaefer and Scornaienchi (2020) and Low et al. (2021).
